# GAC_com.yftech.upgrade.apk

Full Java-readable decompilation of **`com.yftech.upgrade.apk`**, the the OTA client UI — checks, downloads and installs head-unit firmware updates from the [yftech-apks](https://github.com/ammisaidkaidi/yftech-apks) collection.

## 1. What this app is, what it does, and what it is for

`com.yftech.upgrade` is the **over-the-air (OTA) update client** of the YF Tech (GAC) head-unit — the app that shows the "new version available" dialog, downloads the package, verifies it and hands it to the recovery system. It is the **user-facing half** of the upgrade story: the flashing itself is done by `com.yftech.service.upgrade` (which holds `android.permission.RECOVERY`), while this app owns the **network** side — talking to YF Tech's OTA servers over HTTPS, choosing between the domestic and overseas endpoints, managing the Wi-Fi connection used for the download, and rendering progress in a full-screen UI (`AppThemeFullScreen`). It is system-UID, persistent, and it registers an exported receiver for **`android.intent.action.REBOOT`** so the system can trigger the reboot-into-recovery step.

**Purpose / why it exists on the device:**

A head-unit must be updatable in the field without a workshop visit, and it must be updatable over whatever connection is available (T-Box/4G, or the Wi-Fi hotspot the car or the driver's phone provides). This APK is the single client for that flow: it resolves which vehicle project it is running on (so it asks the server for the right firmware), checks for updates, downloads `update.zip` (the Android system image) and `mcuupgrade.bin` (the MCU firmware), verifies both against their `.md5` sidecar files, stores them under `/sdcard/upgrade/`, and then asks the upgrade service to apply them. It also carries a Wi-Fi picker (`wifi/WiFiActivity`, `WiFiDialog`, `WiFiAdapter`) so the driver can connect to a hotspot from inside the upgrade flow.

**How it works (runtime flow):**

1. `MainApplication` starts the process; `MainService` runs the background update check, and `MainReceiver` (exported, action `android.intent.action.REBOOT`) handles the reboot request that finalises an OS update.
2. `data/Config` defines the endpoints: **`https://otapi.yftech.com`** (domestic), **`https://gacota.yftech.com`** (overseas/export — note the `gacota` name), **`http://192.168.28.119`** (internal test server), all serving the path `/ota/checkUpdate`. `ProjectManager.isAbroadProject()` picks between them.
3. `data/ProjectManager` + `data/ProjectInfo` identify the vehicle project (name + `mOSDeviceId` + `mMcuDeviceId`) so the server returns the correct firmware set. `Config.getBrand()` / `getBrandExt()` (`ro.product.brand_ext`) report the brand.
4. `data/UpgradeInfo` / `DownloadRecord` / `TaskState` / `HttpRequestCell` / `HttpRespondCell` model the update task; `manager/DownloadManager` performs the HTTP download with `utils/OKHttp3Utils` (bundled OkHttp 3 + Okio), writing `update.zip`, `update.md5`, `mcuupgrade.bin`, `mcuupgrade.md5` into `UPGRADE_DIR = /sdcard/upgrade/`, with `DOWNLOAD_BUFFER_SIZE = 8192` and `FILE_BUFFER_SIZE = 61440`.
5. Integrity is verified with **MD5** against the `.md5` sidecars before anything is applied.
6. `manager/VersionManagerGlobal` compares the local version against the server's, `manager/UpgradeManagerGlobal` drives the state machine, `manager/WindowManagerGlobal` + `UpgradeViewManager` render the full-screen progress UI, and `manager/CarStateManager` gates the whole flow on the car being powered/awake (an update must not start while driving).
7. `manager/WiFiManagerGlobal` + the `wifi/` package (`WiFiActivity`, `WiFiDialog`, `WiFiAdapter`, `WiFiItem`, `WiFiSecurity`) scan, rank by signal and connect to a Wi-Fi network so a large download can proceed.
8. `data/Config.CONFIG_FILE_NAME = "upgrade.cfg"` persists the local configuration.

**Notable findings:**

- **Live production OTA endpoints are hard-coded**: `https://otapi.yftech.com/ota/checkUpdate` (domestic China) and `https://gacota.yftech.com/ota/checkUpdate` (overseas — the `gacota` host confirms GAC ownership). A **test server `http://192.168.28.119` is also compiled in** and is selected by the same flag — plain HTTP, internal RFC1918 address, reachable only on the YF Tech office/plant network.
- `usesCleartextTraffic="true"` — deliberately allowed, because of that test server.
- The **exported `MainReceiver` listens for `android.intent.action.REBOOT`** with no permission guard: any app on the device can ask this package to reboot the head-unit (it presumably filters on state, but the receiver itself is exported).
- Integrity checking is **MD5 only** — no signature verification of the update package is visible in this APK; the cryptographic trust decision is made server-side or by the upgrade service.
- Permissions include `WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS`, `NETWORK_SETTINGS`, `MOUNT_UNMOUNT_FILESYSTEMS`, `READ_FRAME_BUFFER` (used for screenshots in the UI) and `MODIFY_AUDIO_SETTINGS` (update-complete chime).
- It requests five `com.yftech.permission.*` signature permissions (`service.main.input`, `service.main.audio`, `service.main.screen`, `service.car`, `service.transfer.phonelink`) — it is a client of `com.yftech.service.main` and of the phone-link service, but it declares none of its own.
- Tech stack: RxJava 3, Kotlin stdlib, AndroidX, OkHttp 3 + Okio, plus a copy of `com.yftech.btphone.lib` (the MVP framework lifted from the Bluetooth-phone app).
- Only ~37 YF Tech classes (2,500 lines) — the other ~2,750 Java files are RxJava/Kotlin/OkHttp/Okio/AndroidX.
- Depends on vendor frameworks absent from the APK: `com.yftech.car.permission.CarPermission` and the car services from `com.yftech.service.main`.
